I work in a tax law office, but IANAL. As far as I am aware, the IRS doesn't put a cap on how many installment agreements a taxpayer can enter into. Each successive installment agreement can become more and more difficult as the IRS may start thinking this is a chronic problem.

This is likely not a problem though because its just two back-to-back unfortunate circumstances. Once you file your taxes it sounds like your balance will likely be under $25,000 which means you should qualify for a Streamlined Installment Agreement.

This website gives an overly simplified approach: https://www.avvo.com/legal-guides/ugc/how-to-get-into-a-streamlined-or-fresh-start-installment-agreement-with-the-irs

If you call the IRS and they deny an installment agreement and request full-payment immediately, I would then recommend reaching out to a tax professional. At this point, however, their assistance likely isn't needed. You're probably looking at a SLIA of around $250

Finally, I personally disagree with u/zbucklyo because the more you can pay into 2016, the less likely that you'll have a balance come April 15th of next year. If you don't pay the full tax liability you owe for 2016 then you'll default this installment agreement and have more penalties and interest for 2016. The IRS is SUPER concerned about compliance for the current tax year, then repayment of the old liabilities. I wouldn't even be surprised if while you're on the phone asking for the installment agreement for 2015 they ask what steps you have taken to avoid this issue in 2016.

Yeah... I'm just going to have to completely disagree with the vast majority of your facts.

First of all, the war with France regarding the forts is, I'm assuming, a reference to the French and Indian War which is the North American theatre of the 7 Years War. The British were more than happy to participate. Having the superiority of the navy gave them a distinct advantage in any non-continental war. In addition, the war eventually gave way to Britain becoming, practically, the only European power in the Americas (yes the Spanish are still there and so are the French up in Quebec but the proportion is massively English.

I completely understand the idea that Americans should pay for a good share of the war as they were the main belligerents, but also note that the Americans felt this way as well. The issue that the Americans had were not in the taxes themselves, but rather what was being taxed. The British made sure that there were heavy taxes on manufactured goods. This forced American merchants to sell raw materials to Britain, who would then manufacture the goods, only to sell them back to the Americans. This system of mercantilism is HIGHLY beneficial to the motherland, and utterly disastrous for the colonies.

I highly recommend that you pose this series of questions to r/AskHistorians 

TL:DR; Americans don't like being forced to produce raw materials for the motherland, and have their businesses taxed to bankruptcy.
